0201-playfair-northam.title: Exports & Imports to and from all North-America
0201-playfair-northam.caption: Playfair's chart of “Exports & Imports to and from all North-America,” from the third edition of The Commercial and Political Atlas (1801).
0201-playfair-northam.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia, www.librarycompany.org.
0201-playfair-northam.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library Company of Philadelphia.
0201-playfair-northam.altText: A line graph that tracks exports leaving and imports arriving in North America. The vertical Y axis measures money in millions, and the horizontal X axis measures years in increments of ten from 1700 to 1800. Exports peak at 4.5 million in 1771 and again in 1800 at 4.8 million, while imports gradually increase from 400,000 to 1.8 million between 1700 and 1776, hitting another peak at 3.2 million in the year 1800. When the lines cross and exports exceed imports, Playfair shades the intersection in green to show the “balance in favour of England.” When they cross between 1700 and 1745, imports exceed exports, and the area is shaded in red to show monetary deficit.

0203-playfair-scotland.title: Exports and Imports of Scotland to and from different parts for one Year from Christmas 1780 to Christmans 1781
0203-playfair-scotland.caption: The bar chart included in the first edition of Playfair's Commercial and Political Atlas, considered one of the first examples of the bar chart form.
0203-playfair-scotland.notes: Need to request scan from LCP but their website says to check back in April: https://librarycompany.org/using-the-library/rightsrepro/
0203-playfair-scotland.altText: A horizontal bar graph that measures imports and exports from Scotland for a year, from 1780 to 1781. The vertical y-axis labels names of places, and the horizontal x-axis measures the amount of imports and exports by every ten thousand pounds. Each location has two bars, one shaded in black that represents exports, and another that is lighter (which Playfair labels as “Ribbed) , which tracks imports. The only bars that stretch beyond the midway point of the chart are for the following locations, which increase in imports and exports as the list goes on: the West Indies, America, Russia, and Ireland. There is a noticeably wide gap between the large amount of exports from Scotland to Russia compared to the tiny amount of imports from Russia.

0204-playfair-pie.title: Chart Representing the Extent, Population & Revenues, of the Principal Nations in Europe, after the Division of Poland & Treaty of Luneville
0204-playfair-pie.caption: Playfair's "Chart Representing the Extent, Population & Revenues, of the Principal Nations in Europe, after the Division of Poland & Treaty of Luneville," published in The Statistical Breviary (1801). The pie charts included in this volume are considered the first presently known.
0204-playfair-pie.altText: A chart of twelve multicolored circles line the bottom of a chart and decrease in size from left to right. The chart details the extent, population, and revenues of various European nations, beginning with the Russian Empire, the largest circle, to Portugal, the smallest. Each circle is cut through in half by a horizontal line, which also serves as the bottom line of the vertical Y axis that measures square miles by the million, from 1 to 30 million. Russia’s circle, colored in green, contains within it a smaller pink circle to depict the territories of the empire in the European continent (green) and the Asian continent (pink), where the empire controlled in total 4,720,000 square miles of land after the Treaty of Luneville and the division of Poland. The next circle, showing the Turkish territories, resembles a pie chart divided into three slices of pink, green, and yellow, which depict the territories the empire controlled in Europe, Asia, and Africa (respectively), totalling to 700,000 square miles. The next two circles are, first, Sweden, colored in green, and, second, territories the map calls “Emperor’s Possessions” or “Dominions,” colored in pink, which amount to 209,000 and 204,000 square miles, respectively. France is next, with a pink outer circle and green inner circle to show the different continents (Asian and European, same as above) in which the empire has territories, which in total square miles comes to 182,000. Denmark (pink), Germany (pink, yellow, and green, like the Turkish empire), and Spain (green) follow, controlling 170,000, 168,000, and 148,000 square miles, respectively. Great Britain (green), Prussia (pink), countries under the power of the French (green), and Portugal (green) remain, with total square miles in each empire’s control being 105,000, 90,000, 80,000, and 27,000, respectively. From each circle, except the second smallest circle of countries in the power of the French, two lines extend vertically from their diameters, one higher than the other, and a dotted line connects the tip of each to demonstrate the difference between population and revenue.

0212-minard.title: Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l'armee française dans la campagne de Russie 1812-1813 comparées à celle d'Hannibal durant la 2ème Guerre Punique
0212-minard.caption: Charles Minard's 1869 chart of Napoleon's failed Russia campaign.
0212-minard.creditLine: Courtesy of the Bibliothèque nationale de France
0212-minard.notes: Academic use is free. Can pay for higher-res version if necessary (E60)
0212-minard.altText: A line graph by Charles Minard inspired by Playfair. The graph’s descriptive text is in French. The title translates to “the losses of the French army in the Russian campaign from 1812-1813.” Two thick, jagged horizontal lines dominate the graph. A beige line is thickest and top-most on the graph, decreasing in thickness as the line moves right, indicating movement across Russia. Underneath the beige line, a black line decreases in thickness as the line moves left, indicating retreating movement from Russia by Napoleon’s army. Both lines hit various peaks and valleys, but only intersect at “Polotsk.”

0213-periscopic.title: US Gun Deaths in 2013
0213-periscopic.caption: A screenshot of an animated visualization of the "stolen years" of people killed by guns in the United States in 2013, by the design firm Periscopic.
0213-periscopic.altText: A webpage displaying a vibrant orange line graph against a black backdrop to represent deaths related to gun violence in the United States in 2013. In the top left corner, the number 11,419 is bolded in orange to connect to the amount of orange lines on the graph. The graph takes on a semi-circle shape, arching upwards and bowing towards the middle, which is when the lines fade into a gray color, corresponding to the number in the top right corner, 502,025, which represents the number of years stolen. The horizontal x-axis, the only unit of measurement explained, shows age from 0 to 108. The orange lines—the number of people killed—are overwhelmingly focused in the first half of the graph, highlighting the danger guns pose to children in particular.

0215-playfair-indies.title: Chart of the Exports and Imports to and from the West Indies from the Year 1700 to 1780 by W Playfair
0215-playfair-indies.caption: Playfair's chart of “Exports and Imports to and from the West Indies,”  from the third edition of The Commercial and Political Atlas (1801).
0215-playfair-indies.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia, www.librarycompany.org.
0215-playfair-indies.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library Company of Philadelphia.
0215-playfair-indies.altText: An antique line graph titled "EXPORTS & IMPORTS to and from the WEST INDIES" with the subtitle "Balance Against England." The graph covers the years from 1700 to 1800 on the x-axis (labeled "Time") and money in millions of pounds on the y-axis (labeled "Money"). A yellow line represents Imports. A red line represents Exports. The shaded red area between the import and export lines is labeled "Balance Against England," indicating a trade deficit. The point where the lines cross is marked "Line of Balance." Notable features include a steep increase in imports after mid-century, a dip in the trade deficit around the 1770s, followed by a sharp rise approaching 1800. The graph appears on Plate 4 and includes grid lines for visual reference.

0216-playfair-wheat.title: Chart Showing at One View the Price of the Quarter of Wheat, & Wages of Labour by the Week, from the Year 1565 to 1821
0216-playfair-wheat.caption: One of Playfair's most iconic images, "Chart Showing at One View the Price of the Quarter of Wheat, & Wages of Labour by the Week, from the Year 1565 to 1821," published in 1822. The chart's representation of the price of wheat is among the first bar charts presently known. (The bar charts included in Playfair's Commercial and Political Atlas are believed to be the first.).
0216-playfair-wheat.altText: A historical chart that combines bar and line graph styles to compare the price of wheat to weekly wages mechanics made from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. The chart’s horizontal X axis measures the year from 1565 to 1821 in five year divisions, and the vertical Y axis measures the price of the quarter of wheat in shillings, also counted by five from 0 to 100 shillings. The years are separated by century and further subdivided by England’s monarchy (from earliest to latest: Elizabeth, James I, Charles I, Cromwell, Charles II, James II, William and Mary, Anne, George I, George II, George III, and George IV). Below the differing prices of wheat, which are drawn in grayscale bars likening a silhouetted cityscape, a horizontal red line shows the “weekly wages of a good mechanic.” This line, increasing steadily as the years go by, never surpasses even the lowest points of the price of wheat.

0218-wood.title: Screenshot of Playfair's chart of wheat vs. wages recreated with Observable Plot.
0218-wood.caption: Screenshot of Playfair's chart of wheat vs. wages recreated by Jo Wood using Observable Plot.
0218-wood.altText: A historical chart that combines bar and line graph styles to compare the price of wheat to weekly wages mechanics made from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. The chart’s horizontal X axis measures the year from 1565 to 1821 in five year divisions, and the vertical Y axis measures the price of the quarter of wheat in shillings, also counted by five from 0 to 100 shillings. The years are separated by century and further subdivided by England’s monarchy (from earliest to latest: Elizabeth, James I, Charles I, Cromwell, Charles II, James II, William and Mary, Anne, George I, George II, George III, and George IV). Below the differing prices of wheat, which are drawn in grayscale bars likening a silhouetted cityscape, a horizontal red line shows the “weekly wages of a good mechanic.” This line, increasing steadily as the years go by, never surpasses even the lowest points of the price of wheat.

0224-playfair1787.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia, www.librarycompany.org.
0224-playfair1787.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library Company of Philadelphia.
0224-playfair1787.altText: A line graph that depicts the difference in amount between imports and exports to and from North America between 1700 and 1780. The vertical Y-axis measures imports and exports from 200,000 to 5.8 million, and the horizontal X-axis tracks time every ten years, beginning with 1700 to the far left and ending with 1800. The line for exports remains beneath the line for imports, even as they both gradually rise, from 1700 to about 1747. The line for exports then exceeds imports, shooting up dramatically from 800,000 to 4.6 million in 1770, the peak of the graph. The two lines briefly invert again around the 1775 year mark as exports take a dip to one million, but soon the amount of exports becomes greater than imports, reaching 1.8 million in 1746, and imports plunges from 1.8 million to 200,000 and stays there for the remaining years measured. The difference in the amount of imports and exports is always shaded in gray between the two lines.

0225-jevons002.caption: Two sketches by William Stanley Jevons ca. 1860-61 are all that remain of the charts he created for his statistical atlas. They were deposited in his archive by John Maynard Keynes
0225-jevons002.creditLine: Images courtesy of the Marshall Library of Economics, University of Cambridge.
0225-jevons002.altText: An intricate timeline of line graphs and dots that map various economic enterprises from 1710 to 1850. While most sections are separate to measure each trend individually, the area of some graphs overlaps with others, as if, for instance, the number of patents actually touches (or interacts with) the sectors of banking and the employment of steam.

0226-jevons001.caption: [ SEE ABOVE ]
0226-jevons001.creditLine: Images courtesy of the Marshall Library of Economics, University of Cambridge.
0226-jevons001.altText: Multiple line graphs tracing the number and prices of livestock and farming equipment. The space between lines are shaded in red or blue to distinguish the differences between prices in, for example, butter, cheese, beer, as with the bottom-most graph, or hay, salt, straw, and clover, as with the second chart from the top. Each of the four line graphs (stacked vertically) exhibits an upward trend moving along the horizontal x-axis, though all but the top graph also slope downward at the right-end of the sheet.
